title: Toward unity
hook: Catholics and Orthodox continue dialogue and marked 1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascha: a dark church, one flame, and a greeting shouted back at the doors. Your line was truly he is risen.

Two old men in long robes walk toward each other in Jerusalem. One is the bishop of Rome, the other the patriarch of Constantinople. Their churches have been divided a long time, with excommunications on the books, hurt on both sides, and a long habit of not speaking. They don't sign a treaty or settle a single doctrine. They embrace, and exchange a kiss of peace, the way the liturgy does it. A small gesture. Afterward, the old excommunications are lifted, and the two churches begin talking in earnest.
screen: `TWO OLD MEN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO TREATY. AN EMBRACE.` → `THE OLD EXCOMMUNICATIONS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: At the supper before his arrest, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims, "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." The Catholic Church takes that prayer as a task, not a wish. Catholics and Orthodox already share a great deal: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, the Creed of Nicaea, the early councils, the Mother of God, the saints, the icons. They have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together, remembering a creed they both still pray. What divides them is real too, above all the role of the bishop of Rome, and it is worked on slowly, in official dialogue, by theologians from both sides. Then the honest part. Eastern Catholic churches speak of themselves as a sign that East and West can share one communion. Some Orthodox see them differently, as a wound from the past. Catholic and Orthodox theologians have said together that bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today. Both views are held by people of good faith. Last, what's in reach now. Paul writes, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." Catholics and Orthodox can pray for each other, visit each other, learn each other's hymns, and greet each other at Pascha with the same words. The day of full communion isn't here. But the embrace came first, before any agreement, and the road starts there.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · `SO MUCH ALREADY SHARED.` · `THE HONEST PART: TWO VIEWS.` · `THE EMBRACE CAME FIRST.` · then, large: `ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, picture a Latin church you know: the altar, the pews, the crucifix. On the out-breath, picture one of the Eastern churches from these days, a wall of icons, a priest's family, a cedar, a candle passed hand to hand, and keep breathing between the two, letting neither crowd out the other. If you pray, pray Jesus's own words, that they all may be one; if you don't, hold both pictures side by side, at peace.
Toward unity. The long work of Catholics and Orthodox to become one communion again, through prayer, dialogue and friendship, begun with an embrace. Today's word.
Your line: one day together. Tomorrow a new stretch begins: devotions. That's today, done.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church takes part in official theological dialogue with the Orthodox churches, and popes and patriarchs meet, pray together and exchange delegations on their churches' patronal feasts; Catholics pray for Christian unity, including during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

chat.says: Are Catholics and Orthodox ever going to be one church again?
options: Not yet. They share a great deal, keep talking in official dialogue, and pray that they all may be one.
They already are. The split ended for good on the day the pope and patriarch embraced.
Never. Their churches stopped speaking centuries ago, and they still don't talk to each other.
chat.meaning: Full communion isn't here yet. Catholics and Orthodox share much, keep up official dialogue, and pray Jesus's prayer that they all may be one.

patriarch.meaning: the title of a senior bishop in the Eastern churches

Constantinople.meaning: the ancient city now called Istanbul

excommunications.meaning: formal sentences cutting someone off from a church's communion

Nicaea.meaning: the city of the early council that gave the Creed

notes: Index hook: '1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025'. Script omits the number and year under the claims rule ('Catholics and Orthodox have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together'). Confirm, including Pope Leo XIV's visit to Nicaea (İznik) with Patriarch Bartholomew in late 2025 if the editor wants it named.

The Jerusalem embrace of Paul VI and Athenagoras (January 1964) and the lifting of the 1054 excommunications (December 1965) are told without names in the hook and without dates. Confirm 'afterward' sequencing and the kiss of peace detail.
'Their churches have been divided for centuries': confirm.
Balamand statement (1993) summarized as 'bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today'; confirm the paraphrase.
Orthodox view of Eastern Catholic churches 'as a wound from the past' and Eastern Catholic self-understanding presented side by side, unranked. Confirm fairness to both.
'Catholics and Orthodox share the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles' reflects Unitatis Redintegratio 15; confirm wording.
Douay-Rheims wording of John 17:21 and Ephesians 4:5: confirm.
